comments.author: TeMPOraL
comments.why: Well-reasoned theory of em-dash overuse from quality-weighted training data plus AI-detection heuristics.
comments.text: My pet theory is that this was happening, because labs naturally worked to source highest quality data sources they could get. Even if they initially slurped everything indiscriminately, the obvious next step is to sort them by "quality", and bias towards the high end while trimming from low end. So obviously, government documents, top publications from liberal arts scholars and STEM > Wikipedia > Reddit (and within, r/AskHistorians > r/all, etc.). The first group is the one most likely to (over)use correct / fancy typography. I have a related pet theory: the telltale sign of AI writing is being too good for the context it's found in , in terms of vocabulary and style as well as structure. What is jarring about this is precisely the quality - we associate certain styles with important (or self-important) venues, so it's uncanny to suddenly see random shitposts, copywriting spam, or regular chat replies look like work of NYT bestselling authors or legal scholars - it feels wrong in places we expect basic language, grug-brain reasoning, and lots of typos. Also, what makes the above much more noticeable, is that AI systems don't have cross-session stylistic memory. From the POV of an LLM, that perfectly fitting, masterfully crafted starter is the first and only time it used it. From the user's POV, it's the tenth time they're seeing it in the span of an hour.

comments.author: TeMPOraL
comments.why: Long, detailed explanation of chat-mode vs agentic-mode capability differences with concrete examples and links.
comments.text: > Everyone says that until ms, apple, google, etc introduces this polished feature as part of their tablet imaging editing/document collaboration office suite. Then everyone can;t get enough of it. I don't feel like I'm a representative sample of general userbase, so I won't dispute this too hard. For me, it's rare but it does happen. Still, 90% of my mobile experience is "how is this so broken, why is it missing the obvious follow-up feature that completes a workflow, and why, again, am I not using a laptop for this?". > If it's a small task then why can't LLMs actually do it? What if they actually can? This is exactly what Karpathy was talking about the other day[0]. If your only LLM experience is the default chat app in chat mode, then this doesn't make sense. If your experience includes using agentic harness like Claude Code/Cowork / Codex/ChatGPT Work, then it's obvious. The LLM app in "chat mode" will just zero-shot you a pelican, or digitize your notes into SVG, and maybe improve on it a bit if you complain about the result. The same app[1] in "agentic mode" will digitize your notes, refine the SVG against the original image, reduce it to probable strokes based on high-frequency patterns in the photo and knowledge of how people write, OCR it, save both the text and SVG to your library, then extract parts you wanted and insert them into a document, typeset the rest of it, and print it on your printer - all in response to a single prompt. LLMs in agentic mode are very good at stringing long and advanced workflows; today, if you give them shell access or computer use, they will use regular apps for you if that's the easiest way to accomplish the goal. > Have you actually tried this? Yes![2]. That's why I can confidently say: there is no limit to this pattern. LLMs can handle apps just fine; giving them tools just saves time and tokens . Another example: I'm currently resurrecting a 30 year old game, and the other day I asked Claude to hack on a way to run it headlessly, so I can use my computer while it plays with it. It did, and then immediately leveraged it to just causally run several instances of the game in parallel, entirely in the background, whenever it needed to playtest something. -- [0] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50047422 - was on the frontpage two days ago. [1] - Claude and ChatGPT now have both modes in their mobile, web and desktop apps. I personally use Claude Code a lot, but exclusively through these surfaces (I can't be arsed to deal with TUI at home anymore). IMO, these tools are already within reach of regular users - the users just didn't notice it yet. [2] - Not with SVGs, but equivalent with voice recordings, and yes, Claude Code set up and is managing the whole local processing pipeline. Recordings go in, Markdown (or more advanced signal processing) comes out, and in itself, it's not a task, but merely a step .

comments.author: isityettime
comments.why: Detailed technical analysis of Android assistant APIs and Pixel NPU access restrictions as anticompetitive leverage.
comments.text: On Android, the public APIs available for digital assistants are more limited than the ones that Google gets to use for their own products. So if you want a digital assistant and you'd like to be able to hold a button on your phone and have it open a thread with an LLM (even if your screen is off), your digital assistant has to be Gemini. You can configure ChatGPT or Claude in its place, but then they can't manipulate or interact with apps in your phone very much. Or you can use an app like that for all of your LLM use but you can't conveniently summon it. Similarly, you can run local LLMs on your Google Pixel smartphone, but if you want them to be hardware accelerated using the chip that's included for that very purpose on your phone... it has to be Google's models via Google's apps. So you can't say "alright, a fast, local model which sounds great, but I want one that is trained to always run a search before answering, in a harness with good search tools for answering the kinds of practical questions I often ask", you're actually not free to put that together in a practicable way. So there is indeed some competition here. But it's not really fair competition.

comments.author: sebmellen
comments.why: Highly concrete medical-imaging use case (OCT/RNFL) with numbered model behaviors and an artifact link.
comments.text: It’s wild how good it is at explaining nuanced and complex health topics. As an example, I recently had an OCT scan of my retina because I'm a “glaucoma suspect.” I'm a glaucoma suspect because I have an unusually high cup-to-disc ratio, which is a pattern typically seen in glaucomatous patients. As part of this OCT scan, you get a report back on your RNFL, which is basically a report on the health and thickness of your optic nerve(s) and retina(s). (Dramatically oversimplifying, of course.) My ophthalmologist struggled to explain my OCT scan results to me and instead sort of shrugged and said, "It's probably because you're a high myope, but we'll keep you coming in once a year.” But my scans look horrifically bright red — meaning I'm in less than the first percentile of retinal thickness for my age. Obviously concerning enough to do my own research… ChatGPT 6 Pro and Opus 5.5 have struggled to make any sense of the clinical implications of these scans. In contrast, Argon was the first model to: 1. explain how the OCT machine works 2. detail the physiological mechanism that causes the cupping and thinner RNFL layers in my scenario 3. sum it up into a clinical recommendation (similar to what my ophthalmologist recommended, with the addition of basic supplementation and lifestyle modification changes) 4. provide an interactive visualization of the topography of my eye vs a glaucomatic eye: https://optic-nerve-3d.netlify.app/ I'm blown away.

comments.text: To be honest I’m not sure - the tooling around it has processes to start things, and gourds around tool usage to remind Claude of proper procedure. But ultimately I find it a silver lining more than a problem. I am building and changing tooling so fast, and the models tooling itself is changing so fast, that by the time I establish a workflow, I either A) have solved the original problem so no longer needed, B) have built other tooling that distorts the picture, or C) the labs have released something new and cool that changes the equation drastically so your previous setup is gone anyway. For example I built some procedure on how to split work between fable and opus and sonnet to optimise token usage, then opus 5.5 came along and made all of this obsolete. Not per “token usage” mind you, opus is still expensive, but more “effort per task time finish” kind of metric. If I want to close things faster while still being relatively within budget, it is just easier to send all to opus - it will now just solve thigns quicker so you still use similar amount of tokens / money, but quicker, which is a trade I’ll make any day. And every time “the system is working” I either just stumble onto the next resource constraint, or I feel uncomfortable and start refactoring to make things better and inevitably destabilise the whole “machine”
